title: Convergence, WLLN, SLLN and CLT
engineName: Probability — convergence, laws and normal limits
objectives: Distinguish almost-sure, in-probability and distributional convergence.
State weak and strong laws with their assumptions.
Use Chebyshev's inequality to establish convergence in probability.
Apply the central limit theorem to sample means and sums.
Interpret the CLT as an asymptotic law for scaled errors, not an exact finite-sample identity.

prereq.name: Random variables and distribution functions
prereq.why: Define convergence through distributions and events.

traps: Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability, but not conversely in general.
WLLN concerns convergence in probability; SLLN concerns almost-sure convergence.
CLT concerns the scaled error, not the unscaled sample mean.
Use σ/√n as the standard error, not σ²/n.
The finite-variance CLT is asymptotic, not an exact finite-sample normal law.
Chebyshev gives an upper bound; it is not a normal approximation.

sheet: X_n→X a.s. means sample paths converge except on a null set.
X_n→X in probability iff P(|X_n−X|>ε)→0 for every ε>0.
X_n⇒X means CDF convergence at continuity points.
Almost sure ⇒ in probability ⇒ in distribution.
tricks: Identify the mode before selecting a theorem.
For the mean use σ/√n, not σ²/n.
Separate a bound from an approximation.
shortcuts: For n=100, standard error is σ/10.
For a two-sided CLT interval, standardise both endpoints.
remember: LLN is about the average; CLT is about its scaled error.
Distributional convergence does not imply probability convergence.

howto: Underline the mode of convergence before selecting a theorem. WLLN is in probability, SLLN is almost sure, and CLT is in distribution for a scaled error. Keep Chebyshev bounds separate from normal approximations.

provenance: Original syllabus-aligned lesson authored 12 November 2026. Standard errors, Chebyshev bounds and CLT standardisations were checked algebraically. The X_n=(-1)^nX example is a direct counterexample to the converse from distributional to probability convergence. No PYQ attribution is claimed.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four foundations
body: Convergence describes what happens to a sequence of random variables as n grows.
Three modes are central: almost sure, in probability and in distribution. WLLN and SLLN describe averages; CLT describes scaled fluctuations.

ask.q: What is the standard error of an iid sample mean?
ask.nudge: Divide the population SD by square root n.

refresh: Convergence in probability means P(|X_n−X|>ε) tends to zero for every ε>0. It controls the probability of a fixed-size deviation, not necessarily the expectation or every realised sample path. Translate the definition before applying a theorem.

Almost-sure convergence means the event that X_n converges to X has probability one. It is stronger than convergence in probability, which is stronger than convergence in distribution under the usual conditions. Do not reverse these implications without additional assumptions.

The weak law of large numbers gives convergence of the sample mean to the population mean in probability under suitable conditions such as iid observations with finite variance. The strong law gives almost-sure convergence under its own assumptions. Always state which law and which moment conditions are being used.

items.recall: Subtract the mean and divide by the SD.
refresh: The central limit theorem standardises the sum or sample mean and gives an asymptotic normal distribution under suitable conditions. It is not an assertion that the original observations are normal, nor does it make a small-sample distribution exactly normal.

scenes.title: The average stabilises; the scaled error remains random
body: The law of large numbers says that the sample average approaches the population mean.
The central limit theorem does not contradict this. It rescales the shrinking error by √n, revealing a non-degenerate normal limit.
The standard error shrinks as σ/√n, while the scaled error has a limiting distribution.

scenario.teaser: A factory average is stable even though individual fills remain variable.
scenario.title: The average is not an individual item
body: A process has mean fill 500 ml and SD 12 ml. A sample of 144 items is taken.
The standard error of the sample mean is 12/√144=1 ml. By the CLT, the probability that the sample mean lies between 498 and 502 is approximately P(−2<Z<2)=0.9545.
This is not the probability that an individual item lies between 498 and 502 ml. Individual variability remains 12 ml; averaging reduces the SD by √n.
The LLN says the average settles near 500; the CLT quantifies the remaining error at the 1 ml scale.
scenario.q: Why is the sample mean less variable than an individual observation?
scenario.answer: Var(X̄_n)=σ²/n, so its SD is σ/√n; the individual SD remains 12 ml.

ask.q: What does the LLN say that the CLT does not?
ask.nudge: One is convergence to a constant; the other is a distribution for the scaled error.

blocks.body: Almost surely: P(lim X_n=X)=1. In probability: P(|X_n−X|>ε)→0 for every ε>0. In distribution: F_n(x)→F(x) at continuity points of F.
Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence in distribution. The converses are false in general.
For iid X_i with finite mean μ, X̄_n→μ in probability. Finite variance gives a short Chebyshev proof: Var(X̄_n)=σ²/n.
For iid variables with E|X₁|<∞, X̄_n→μ almost surely. This is stronger than convergence in probability.
For iid variables with finite positive variance σ², √n(X̄_n−μ)/σ⇒N(0,1). Equivalently (S_n−nμ)/(σ√n)⇒N(0,1).
It is asymptotic, not an exact finite-n normal law. It does not say individual observations become normal or that the unscaled average has a random normal limit.

scenes.title: Worked example — a sample mean
scenes.objective: Use the CLT with the correct standard error.
scenes.problem: An iid population has mean 50 and SD 10. For n=100, approximate P(49<X̄<51) using the CLT.

steps.why: Use SD divided by square root n, not the population SD.
This is approximate unless the parent population is normal.

scenes.after: The CLT approximation is not exact unless the parent population is normal.

ask.q: What is the standard error in this example?

items.a: Almost sure ⇒ in probability ⇒ in distribution.

scenes.title: Complete the Chebyshev bound
scenes.objective: Use the variance of the sample mean.
scenes.problem: For iid variables with variance σ², complete the bound for the sample mean.

blank.hint: Independent variances add, then divide by n².

steps.why: This proves convergence in probability under finite variance.

scenes.after: Chebyshev supplies a proof of the WLLN under finite variance.

scenes.title: CLT standardisation and limits
scenes.objective: Apply the CLT to sums and means.

blocks.body: √n(X̄_n−μ)/σ ⇒ N(0,1); equivalently X̄_n is approximately N(μ,σ²/n) for large n.
The classical iid CLT requires finite positive variance. The approximation improves with n but its accuracy depends on the parent distribution, especially skewness and tail weight.

ask.q: Why do we divide by σ/√n rather than σ²/n?
ask.nudge: One is a standard deviation; the other is a variance.

scenes.title: On your own — a second CLT interval
scenes.problem: An iid population has μ=20 and σ²=36. For n=144, use the CLT to approximate P(19.5<X̄<20.5).
scenes.answer: SE=.5; the standardised interval is (−1,1); probability≈.6827.
scenes.check: Use σ=6, not variance 36, in the standard error.

scenario.teaser: A student reverses the implication from convergence in distribution.
scenario.title: Same marginal laws do not force closeness
body: Let X be standard normal and X_n=(−1)^nX. Every X_n has the same standard normal distribution, so X_n converges in distribution to X.
But X_n does not converge in probability to X: for odd n, |X_n−X|=2|X|, which exceeds any fixed small ε with non-vanishing probability.
Thus convergence in distribution controls marginal CDFs, not the closeness of two variables on a common probability space.
Remember the implication ladder: almost sure ⇒ in probability ⇒ in distribution; reverse implications need extra assumptions.
scenario.q: Does convergence in distribution imply convergence in probability?
scenario.answer: No. The marginal laws can converge while the variables remain separated on the probability space.

solution.why: The variance is 36, so SD is 6.

items.claim: Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability.
items.why: True: almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability.

items.claim: Convergence in distribution implies convergence in probability in general.
items.why: False: marginal CDF convergence does not control coupling distance.

items.claim: The WLLN states convergence of the sample mean in probability.
items.why: True: this is the weak law.

items.claim: The SLLN is an almost-sure statement.
items.why: True: the strong law is pathwise.

items.claim: The CLT makes the finite-sample mean exactly normal for every parent law.
items.why: False: the classical CLT is asymptotic.

items.claim: The standard error of the iid sample mean is σ/√n.

scenes.title: Transfer problem — bound versus approximation
scenes.problem: If iid X_i have μ=8 and σ²=25, use Chebyshev to bound P(|X̄_100−8|≥1). Compare with the CLT approximation.
scenes.check: The Chebyshev bound is .25, not .05. A bound and a normal approximation are different.

solution.why: Independent observations divide the variance by n.

solution.math: SE=.5, so threshold is 2 standard errors; P(|Z|≥2)≈.0455
solution.why: This is an approximation, not a guaranteed upper bound.
